figures.caption: Figure 2: The overall architecture of LaS. (a) Prompt Pc is the complete class description supplied to the text encoder. Each task–encoder model trains its neural encoder and projections Wn and Wt for neural–text alignment, then predicts the highest-scoring candidate. (b) The evaluated tasks comprise finger MI and SSVEP decoding from scalp EEG, and overt Chinese word reading from intracranial sEEG. Speech class descriptions use English translations. (c) Neural input representations follow the selected encoder. Subject-specific sEEG tokenizers feed a backbone shared within the same model.

Table 1: Decoding performance across tasks and neural encoders. CLS–LaS comparisons; FBCSP-LDA is a separate MI reference. Performance: subject-mean accuracy (%) ± sample SD; mean MI κ in parentheses. ∆ = LaS − CLS in percentage points. Blue/gray: highest/secondhighest means within each MI or Speech metric across CLS and LaS. 1SSVEP: RW training → IW evaluation. Stars: Holm-corrected paired t-tests within encoder (Section 4.1; Appendix B.6).

Figure 3: Candidate-subset reuse in motor imagery. CLS trains per subtask; LaS restricts candidates in each fold’s four-class checkpoint without further optimization. Class IDs 1, 2, 3, 4 denote Thumb, Index, Middle, Pinky. Boxes: medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs); whiskers: 1.5×IQR rule; circles: subject accuracies (n = 21); diamonds: means; dashed lines: chance (50%/33.3%). Stars: Holm-corrected paired CLS–LaS comparisons (Section 4.1).

Figure 4: Label-supervised adaptation and LaS zero-shot decoding. Neural models in (a,b) are initialized from LaS and adapted using CLS. (a) SSVEP subject adaptation: mean validation accuracy with K target-subject calibration blocks (1-s inputs; six leave-one-block-out rounds). (b) MI session adaptation: adapted-model accuracy on eight later (“Fine”) test runs minus direct-inference accuracy on eight Base runs per subject (mean paired differences across 21 subjects; 95% t intervals). (c) LaS SSVEP decoding restricted to five held-out frequency classes, with the same 35 subjects used for training and evaluation (mean ± SD across eight class splits; 20% chance). The broken axis omits 25–60%; its two segments use different scales.

Figure 5: Training prompt configurations and inference settings. (a) Closed-set decoding. (b) Five-class SSVEP unseen-only decoding with one 1-s initial window; dashed line: 20% chance. Panels (a,b) use fixed prompts at inference. (c) P0 and P2 are evaluated with an ensemble of five templates held out from both training configurations. Units in (a–c): subjects (21 MI, 35 SSVEP, 12 Speech) or eight ZSL class splits. Boxes: medians and IQRs; whiskers follow the 1.5 × IQR rule; hollow circles: outliers; colored symbols: means. Brackets: paired comparisons with P0. (d) EmbeddingGemma−BERT accuracy differences (pp); best configurations are selected independently of the Frozen–LoRA pairs (Figure B.1). Holm-corrected paired tests (Section 4.1).

Figure 6: Dual-sided attribution visualization with Integrated Gradients. Training-trial averages: (a) MI, (b) Speech, and (c) SSVEP. Blue denotes low nonnegative neural display values, not negative attribution; green denotes positive mean word contributions. Separate panel scales preclude absolute comparisons.

Figure 7: Speech training objectives across batch sizes. Du-IN with (a) InfoNCE, (b) Diagonal SigLIP, and (c) Class-aware SigLIP. Colored dots: each seed’s minimum epoch-average full training loss (left axis); gray diamonds: mean accuracy (right axis). Lines show the balanced-class lower bounds in Equation (5), extended continuously to m = B/61. Pale bands and upward point offsets are display aids, not uncertainty. †At B = 1024 in (c), four loss observations are shown; accuracy includes all five seeds. The full three-task comparison appears in Figure B.6.
